items.abstract: Reconstructing terrestrial palaeoenvironmental change during the Middle Pleistocene is essential for understanding ecosystem stability and resilience under long-term climatic forcing. However, well-dated, quantitative records from Australia remain limited. Fossil deposits at Mount Etna Caves, central eastern Queensland, preserve two taxonomically distinct faunal assemblages that have been interpreted as a substantial ecological transition from a diverse rainforest system to an arid-adapted faunal community. Previous interpretations of this transition have relied primarily on faunal evidence, with limited site-specific geochemical validation. Here, we integrate oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) analyses of fossil macropodid enamel with refined in-situ U-Th geochronology to reconstruct changes in hydroclimatic conditions across this transition. New U-Th ages better constrain deposition of the arid-adapted assemblage to a narrow interval between 199 ± 5 and 205 ± 4 ka. Fossils from older deposits (pre-280 ka) exhibit consistently low δ 18 O values (−2.59 ± 0.54 ‰), suggesting relatively humid conditions, whereas the younger deposit is markedly enriched (4.59 ± 1.92 ‰). Random Forest classification models trained on modern macropodine δ 18 O data suggest that pre-280 ka assemblages show strongest similarity with humid temperate forest environments analogous to modern temperate oceanic (Cfb-like) systems of southeastern Australia and highland New Guinea. In contrast, the post-205 ka assemblages show the strongest affinity with arid, hot desert (BWh-like) conditions characteristic of central Australia. This transition coincides with broader Middle Pleistocene climatic reorganisation centred on ∼270 ka, which may have contributed to sustained regional drying. These findings suggest that long-term climatic forcing may push ecosystems beyond hydroclimatic thresholds, resulting in major ecological reorganisation, altered species distributions, and reduced biogeographic connectivity. By providing a directly dated, multi-proxy terrestrial record, this study highlights how substantial environmental change during the Quaternary offers an important analogue for understanding ecosystem vulnerability under ongoing and future climate change.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Environmental on‐site records covering the late La Tène culture in the late 2nd century BC and early 1st century AD are rare in southern Germany. On a local level such records could help to address the question if and when a settlement gap occurred in southern Germany between the late La Tène culture in the late 1st century BC and the onset of Roman colonisation in the late 1st century AD. Various scenarios have been proposed, ranging from complete depopulation of some areas to the collapse of primarily larger settlements accompanied by only a partial decline of land‐use intensity, up to a settlement continuity that remains obscured by taphonomic filters and insufficient typochronological resolution. Precisely dated environmental on‐site records covering the beginning of this time period therefore provide crucial evidence. Here, we present a multi‐proxy analysis (macrobotanical remains, palynology, archaeozoology and entomology) of the sediments within a wooden well structure built after 133 BC in the highly fertile Nördlinger Ries area, Bavaria. The initial record reflects nearby settlement activities, including husbandry and agriculture. A secondary use of the structure for processing of nettle is likely. The upper infill layers provide a pollen sequence that shows a rapid decline of taxa related to human activity, accompanied by species indicative of ecological succession on abandoned patches of land. We conclude that settlement activities in this region declined drastically during the 1st century BC. Our results support the hypothesis of regional depopulation in southern Germany prior to the establishment of the Roman province of Raetia.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Extensive degradation has necessitated high‐priority restoration of UK peatland ecosystems. Palaeoecology has great potential to support peatland restoration, offering a long‐term perspective of environmental change that can help determine baseline conditions, restoration targets, and intervention success. However, it is suggested by palaeoenvironmental researchers that palaeoecology is underutilised in practical settings, with few examples of applied palaeoecological studies within academic literature. This study uses a practice perspective to evaluate the extent to which palaeoecology is incorporated into UK peatland restoration and identifies barriers and opportunities for integrating long‐term ecological research into restoration practice. A desk‐based study of 68 UK peatland restoration projects and survey of 32 peatland practitioners were used to explore the use of palaeoecological research as part of UK peatland restoration projects. A total of 10 instances of applied palaeoecology in UK peatland restoration were found between the desk‐based study and practitioner survey. The findings indicate that palaeoecology is rarely utilised in UK peatland restoration practice, with limitations in funding, time, and academic input identified as key barriers. Cases where palaeoecology has been considered primarily utilised pollen analysis and radiocarbon dating, with practitioners largely involved in fieldwork and research design. This study makes two recommendations to facilitate the incorporation of palaeoecological research into UK peatland restoration practice: (i) better dissemination and documentation of case studies to provide greater evidence of how palaeoecology may be used to support UK peatland restoration and clearer insight into the use of palaeoecology in practice; (ii) better two‐way knowledge transfer between palaeoecologists and practitioners to identify restoration challenges and knowledge gaps where palaeoecology could contribute.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Detailed microstratigraphic analyses have been rare in Australia, and exceptionally so from the temperate southeast. Located in GunaiKurnai Country, southeastern Australia, Cloggs Cave preserves a well‐stratified Late Pleistocene to Holocene archaeological and environmental record, with remarkable evidence for use of the site as a place of ritual practices informed by local cosmologies. Although the geomorphological history of the cave has been well established, here, we present the results of microstratigraphic analyses that identify the key drivers of sedimentation that resulted in the accumulation and preservation of the archaeological deposits in the cave. The stratigraphic sequence tracks a largely dry cave environment, which has led to the high level of organic preservation, despite some minor phosphate‐ and sulphate‐related diagenesis being observed. Micro‐scale evidence traces the Old Ancestors' use of the cave for ~25,000 years, and supports both GunaiKurnai cultural knowledge and independent archaeological evidence that the cave was not an occupation site, but was rather periodically visited for special purposes. Cave sedimentation is driven by alternating cycles of faunal inputs and roof spall that accumulate during periods of human absence, and burning signatures and plant remains that signal the recurrent presence of the Old Ancestors in the cave. The investigation of in situ combustion features suggests low‐temperature burning of soft plant materials, which can be linked to practices known by GunaiKurnai knowledge and ethnography, and reinforces the cosmological value of Cloggs Cave in GunaiKurnai culture.</jats:p>
